name: Talk To Me In Korean
description: A large, well-ordered curriculum of short audio and video lessons (Core Grammar Level 1 has about 26 lessons), plus books and workbooks. Courses now need a paid subscription; the first lesson of a course is a free sample.
why: The clearest step-by-step grammar course for beginners. Worth paying for only if the free options below stop being enough.
note: A TTMIK page says the free Basic membership is being discontinued. Their YouTube channel and podcasts stay free.

name: Talk To Me In Korean (YouTube)
description: About 2,000 free videos: vocabulary, common mistakes, real conversations with subtitles and study tips.
why: Free short videos from the same teachers as the course. Good for a 5-minute listening break.

name: Real-Life Korean Conversations For Beginners (podcast)
description: A free TTMIK podcast of short everyday dialogues for beginners, based on their book of the same name. Also on other podcast apps.
why: Natural beginner dialogues you can play on the bus. Pairs well with the survival stage.

name: How to Study Korean
description: A free text-based course. Unit 0 teaches Hangul; each unit after that has 25 lessons, quizzes and a unit test, with free PDFs. Explanations are long and thorough.
why: The most detailed free grammar explanations. Use it as a reference when a grammar point does not make sense.
note: Lessons are free; workbooks are sold separately.

name: Nuri King Sejong Institute (online)
description: The King Sejong Institute Foundation’s online learning platform, run with government support. Self-study courses from beginner to intermediate, with an English interface. Needs a free account.
why: Official, textbook-quality Korean from the people who run Korean language centres worldwide.
note: Live online classes open in rounds and are limited by country; the self-study courses are the part you can use any time.

name: First Step Korean (Yonsei University, Coursera)
description: A short beginner course from Yonsei University: Hangul, greetings, family, numbers, time and dates, daily-life words. About 6 weeks at 1 to 3 hours a week. Rated about 4.9 by tens of thousands of learners.
why: A compact, well-taught first course that fits the Hangul and core-vocabulary stages exactly.
note: Listed at about $49 or with Coursera Plus. Coursera sometimes offers a free option without a certificate; check the Enroll button.

name: Learn to Speak Korean 1 (Yonsei University, Coursera)
description: Yonsei’s follow-up course for learners who already read Hangul: introducing yourself, your hometown, food, shopping and ordering in a restaurant.
why: The natural next step after First Step Korean, and close to the survival situations you will meet in week one.
note: Included with Coursera Plus. Some reviewers find it lighter than First Step Korean.

name: GO! Billy Korean
description: Billy Go’s free lessons: a numbered Beginner Korean Course, Learn Hangul, a conversation course and full lessons with PDFs. Also sells the Korean Made Simple books.
why: A friendly, structured free path taught by someone who learned Korean as an adult.
note: Lessons are free; the books are paid.

name: GO! Billy Korean (YouTube)
description: The video side of GO! Billy Korean: a long numbered beginner course, free live classes most Sundays and natural conversation videos.
why: Numbered lessons make it easy to track as an active course: one video per day.
note: A different channel uses a similar name; check that it is Billy Go’s.

name: Korean Unnie 한국언니 (YouTube)
description: Short videos by Sohyun, a native speaker, on high-frequency words, everyday expressions and Korean culture. Over a million subscribers.
why: Short and easy to search when you want one word or expression explained.

name: seemile Korean (YouTube)
description: Animated lessons and short stories for beginner and intermediate learners, with several hosts. About 1.7 million subscribers. There is also a seemile app.
why: Light, visual lessons for days when you are tired of textbooks.

name: Korean Englishman 영국남자 (YouTube)
description: Josh and Ollie, two Englishmen who live in Seoul, show Korean food and everyday life, often with Korean friends and guests. Entertainment more than lessons.
why: An easy way to see daily life and food culture in Korea before you arrive.

name: Asian Boss (YouTube)
description: A Seoul-based channel known for street interviews and longer explainers about life and society in Korea and Asia.
why: Hear ordinary Koreans talk about real topics, with subtitles. Good background on society and opinions.
note: Covers social and political topics; opinions in street interviews are individual, not the whole country’s.

name: Naver Dictionary
description: Korea’s most used online dictionary, with a Korean-English dictionary, audio and many example sentences. Also an app.
why: The dictionary Koreans use. Many example sentences show how a word is really used.
note: Pick the Korean-English dictionary on the start page. Some example sentences are user-submitted and not always reliable.

name: Korean-English Learners’ Dictionary (NIKL)
description: The National Institute of Korean Language’s free dictionary for learners: about 50,000 basic words with English translations, written for people learning Korean.
why: Official, careful definitions at learner level. The safest place to check a word.

name: Papago
description: Naver’s translator: text, voice, conversation mode and camera translation of signs and menus. Offline text translation after downloading a language pack.
why: Usually better than general translators for Korean. Download the Korean-English pack before you fly.
note: Offline mode covers text; camera translation probably needs a connection.

name: Anki
description: The classic spaced-repetition flashcard program. Free on Windows, Mac, Linux, Android (AnkiDroid) and the web; the iPhone app is a one-time purchase (about $25).
why: Only needed if you want decks this app does not have. Hangeul Road already does spaced repetition for its words.

name: Forvo
description: A pronunciation dictionary of recordings by native speakers. Many Korean words and phrases; no definitions.
why: Hear a real person say a word when the phone voice sounds wrong.
note: Crowdsourced, so a recording can occasionally be wrong. Listen to two speakers if possible.

name: italki
description: A marketplace of paid one-to-one online lessons. Community tutors (conversation) and professional teachers set their own prices; trial lessons are usually cheaper.
why: The fastest way to get real speaking practice before you land. Even a few lessons help.
note: Korean listings show roughly $5 to $35 per hour. Check the price on each tutor’s profile.

name: HelloTalk
description: A language exchange app: chat with Korean speakers who want to learn your language, with built-in corrections and translation. Free; VIP removes limits and ads.
why: Free daily practice with real Koreans, and a way to meet people before you arrive.
note: Free translations are limited per day. Treat it like any social app: be careful with personal details.

name: Tandem
description: A language exchange app similar to HelloTalk: text, voice and video chat with native speakers. Free; Pro adds unlimited translations and search by city.
why: A second exchange app in case you find better partners here.
note: Use one exchange app at a time, not both.

name: Duolingo
description: The game-style app you already use. The Korean course was rebuilt in 2026 and now has a separate Hangul tab. Free, with an optional subscription.
why: A daily habit you already have. Keep it as a light extra, not your main course.
note: Reviewers agree it rarely makes you conversational on its own.

name: LingoDeer
description: A course app from A1 to B1 with grammar notes, native audio and built-in reviews. The course can be downloaded for offline use. Mostly subscription; some content is free.
why: A more grammar-focused alternative to Duolingo if you want an app course with explanations.
note: Reports differ on how much is free. Try the free lessons before paying.

name: Teuida
description: A speaking app built around first-person video scenes: you answer a Korean speaker out loud and get pronunciation feedback.
why: Speaking practice when no partner is around, in situations like cafes and shops.
note: Teaches mostly set phrases; pair it with a grammar source.

name: The Complete Korean Course for Beginners (Udemy)
description: A bestselling bundle of several beginner courses by Korean Studio. Rated about 4.7 from over 5,000 ratings.
why: One paid package if you like video courses with a fixed order.
note: Honest take: How to Study Korean, GO! Billy Korean and First Step Korean cover the same beginner ground for free or less. Udemy prices drop often during sales.

name: CORE KOREAN 1 (Udemy)
description: A grammar-focused course with a practice and quiz for each of 56 lectures. Rated about 4.6 to 4.7 from about 2,000 ratings. Last updated in 2018.
why: Lots of sentence-building practice if you learn best by drilling patterns.
note: Honest take: older and uses few words; Hangeul Road’s grammar lessons and How to Study Korean cover the same patterns for free.

name: Complete Korean Course: Learn Korean for Beginners (Udemy)
description: A beginner course with over 60,000 students, rated about 4.6 to 4.7 from over 3,000 ratings.
why: A popular alternative if the other Udemy course does not suit you.
note: Honest take: not needed if you follow the free recommended path.

name: Integrated Korean: Beginning 1 (book)
description: A university textbook (3rd edition, 2019) from the KLEAR series, used in many US Korean courses. Free MP3 audio; a separate workbook exists.
why: A real textbook if you want a printed book with a clear order. Optional.
note: List price about $32.

name: TOPIK (official site)
description: The official site of the Test of Proficiency in Korean: test dates by country, registration and results. TOPIK I covers levels 1 and 2. The 2027 schedule has been announced.
why: Optional. A TOPIK I certificate is a nice goal for the end of the semester, not something you need to arrive.
note: The site is free; the test itself has a fee.

name: TOPIK Guide
description: Free TOPIK I and II mock tests built from past papers, with scores and estimated level, plus paid prep courses.
why: Optional. Try one TOPIK I mock test near the end to see where you are.

name: UNIST International Affairs: inbound exchange
description: UNIST’s official pages for incoming exchange students: application, D-2-6 visa, courses (all taught in English), dormitory and student life.
why: Your host university’s own rules and deadlines. Check it for every official step.
note: Inbound questions: inbound@unist.ac.kr.

name: UNIST (official site)
description: The main website of Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology: news, academic calendar, campus information.
why: Campus news and the academic calendar for your semester.

name: Ulsan Metropolitan City (English)
description: The city government’s English site: about Ulsan, city services and contacts for foreign residents.
why: Official information about the city you will live in.

name: Ulsan Tourism (English)
description: The city’s official tourism site: Taehwagang National Garden, Daewangam Park and other sights.
why: Ideas for weekends in Ulsan.
note: Some pages look out of date; check opening times locally.

name: VISITKOREA
description: The Korea Tourism Organization’s official site for foreign visitors: destinations, festivals, transport and travel planning.
why: Reliable official travel information for trips to Busan, Gyeongju and beyond.

name: Korea.net
description: The Korean government’s official portal in English: news, history, culture and society.
why: Official background reading on Korean culture and holidays.

name: Study in Korea
description: The government’s portal for international students, run by NIIED: university search, scholarships, life in Korea and a counselling centre.
why: Official guidance for foreign students on life and paperwork in Korea.
